t: Strong Friendship -- Counting Mutual Friends With a Normalized Edge List
o: Friendship stores each undirected edge exactly once, always with user1_id < user2_id, and a friendship is strong when its endpoints share at least three friends. In the sample, users 1 and 2 share friends {3,4,5,6} (count 4) and users 1 and 3 share {2,6,7} (count 3), so only those two rows qualify; users 2 and 3 share just {1,6} and are excluded. The core difficulty is that each user neighbor set is split across two column positions, so naive self-joins see only half the adjacency unless every edge is first duplicated in both directions. Note that neither endpoint can ever be counted as its own common friend, because the table has no self-edges.
k: A common friend of x and y is a user adjacent to both; neither x nor y can appear in that set because no user befriends themselves.
Duplicating each row as (user1, user2) and (user2, user1) normalizes direction so every adjacency lookup reads one consistent column.
Only pairs already connected in Friendship qualify -- a strong friendship presumes an existing friendship row.

a.n: Approach 1: Expand Each Friendship Into Common-Friend Matches
a.i: Normalize the edge list into a symmetric edges relation, then walk every friendship (x, y): join the neighbors of x against the neighbors of y on the shared friend. Grouping by the friendship pair and keeping groups of size >= 3 yields exactly the strong friendships together with their common-friend counts.
s: Build edges with UNION ALL so each friendship appears in both directions.
Join Friendship f to edges of f.user1_id and edges of f.user2_id sharing the same friend.
Group by the friendship pair and count matches as common_friend.

c.python:
-- Database problem -- the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
WITH edges AS (
    SELECT user1_id AS a, user2_id AS b FROM Friendship
    UNION ALL
    SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship
)
SELECT f.user1_id,
       f.user2_id,
       COUNT(*) AS common_friend
FROM Friendship f
JOIN edges e1 ON e1.a = f.user1_id
JOIN edges e2 ON e2.a = f.user2_id AND e2.b = e1.b
GROUP BY f.user1_id, f.user2_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

a.n: Approach 2: Count Shared Neighbors Per User Pair, Then Require an Edge
a.i: Flip the perspective: join the normalized edges against themselves on the shared center user to enumerate every user pair together with a friend they have in common, normalize each pair with LEAST/GREATEST so user1_id < user2_id, aggregate the counts, and finally keep pairs that are actual friends with at least three shared neighbors.
s: Normalize edges in both directions with UNION ALL.
Self-join edges e1/e2 on the shared center e1.u = e2.u with e1.v <> e2.v.
Aggregate by the LEAST/GREATEST pair to get common_friend per unordered pair.
Join to Friendship to keep genuine friendships and filter common_friend >= 3.

c.python:
-- Database problem -- the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
WITH edges AS (
    SELECT user1_id AS u, user2_id AS v FROM Friendship
    UNION ALL
    SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship
),
pairs AS (
    SELECT LEAST(e1.v, e2.v) AS user1_id,
           GREATEST(e1.v, e2.v) AS user2_id,
           COUNT(*) AS common_friend
    FROM edges e1
    JOIN edges e2 ON e1.u = e2.u AND e1.v <> e2.v
    GROUP BY LEAST(e1.v, e2.v), GREATEST(e1.v, e2.v)
)
SELECT p.user1_id,
       p.user2_id,
       p.common_friend
FROM pairs p
JOIN Friendship f ON f.user1_id = p.user1_id AND f.user2_id = p.user2_id
WHERE p.common_friend >= 3;

a.t: Bounded by the sum of squared degrees during the center-user self-join, plus a linear filter pass
a.sp: O(E + P) -- doubled edges plus one aggregate row per co-friended pair

w: Say out loud that the schema stores each undirected edge once -- that single observation drives the whole normalization. Pitfalls: joining only on the user1_id side misses friendships reachable through user2_id; dropping the e1.v <> e2.v condition inflates counts via degenerate matches; forgetting HAVING >= 3 returns weak pairs too. Duplicate output rows are impossible because the primary key keeps one row per pair. Follow-ups: rank strongest friendships with ORDER BY common_friend DESC, or generalize to at least K mutual friends by parameterizing the threshold.
